result: Monkeys performed a Go/NoGo-countermanding task with behavioral characteristics consistent with the race model of stop-signal tasks. Stop-failure trials had faster RTs than go trials, stop-failure probability increased with switch-signal delay, and the average SSRT was ~160 ms.
evaluation: Claims C19-C24 describe the behavioral task and performance metrics. The data show expected patterns for stop-signal tasks (RT distributions, inhibition functions) with appropriate statistical support (Mann-Whitney U-tests, linear regressions). The SSRT estimates are slightly longer than previous studies but this is acknowledged and explained.

result: 38% of STN neurons (63/167) showed activity changes within the SSRT suitable for involvement in stopping. These included 78% Movement cells (49/63) with truncated movement-related activity and 22% Switch-stop cells (14/63) with phasic increases in firing. Neural cancellation times averaged −55 ms before SSRT.
evaluation: Claims C2, C25-C29, C55 present the core neurophysiological findings with clear quantitative data and appropriate temporal criteria (neural cancellation within SSRT). The ROC analysis method is described and figures support the classification. Sample sizes are adequate for the reported proportions.

result: Switch-stop cells were anatomically segregated to the anterior ventromedial STN, a region known to receive inputs from associative/limbic cortical areas and implicated in impulse control disorders. This anatomical restriction was observed in both animals independently.
evaluation: Claims C3, C30-C32, C94 describe the key anatomical finding shown in Figure 4B. The spatial segregation is clearly demonstrated, replicated across both subjects (C31), and connected to prior anatomical literature (C32). This represents a novel finding at the single-unit level (C94).

result: Of the 14 Switch-stop cells, 57% (8/14) were classified as Stop cells (selective for stopping), while 43% (6/14) were Switch cells (responding similarly to switch-go trials). Neural cancellation times did not differ between Stop and Switch cells.
evaluation: Claims C38-C40, C61 describe further classification of Switch-stop cells based on comparison with switch-go trials. The proportions are clearly stated, the classification criteria are appropriate (comparing responses between conditions), and statistical tests support the lack of timing differences (p=0.66).

result: EMG recordings showed that arm movement inhibition involved rapid relaxation of agonists and brief activation of antagonists. STN neural cancellation times preceded most stop-related EMG changes (30-94 ms) except for the anterior deltoid (−10 ms, p>0.05).
evaluation: Claims C35-C37, C59 present EMG timing data relative to neural activity. While the muscle patterns are clearly shown (Figure 5A), the very short lead time for anterior deltoid (10 ms, non-significant) raises questions about whether STN activity could causally drive the earliest muscle changes. The authors acknowledge this timing constraint but the interpretation remains uncertain.

result: Switch-stop cell activity was not related to eye movements. Regression analyses found no Switch-stop cells (0/14) whose activity encoded eye position or saccade timing, despite the STN containing an oculomotor territory.
evaluation: Claims C41 and C69 address a potential confound. The regression analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) appropriately tests for eye movement correlates using permutation tests (p>0.01). The negative finding is clearly stated and adequately controlled.

result: Torque-responsive neurons (25%, 42/167) were concentrated in dorsal posterolateral STN (skeletomotor territory). These showed minimal overlap with Switch-stop cells (only 1/42 was a Switch cell) and were anatomically distant from the ventromedial region containing Stop/Switch cells.
evaluation: Claims C42-C46, C62 present proprioceptive control data. The spatial segregation between torque-responsive and Switch-stop cells (Figure 7C) is clear, the proportions are well-documented, and the minimal overlap (2%, 1/42) argues against Stop/Switch activity reflecting direct skeletomotor commands.

result: Proactive control was associated with distinct neuronal populations. Go cells (37%, 61/167) and NoGo cells (25%, 41/167) showed differential delay period activity but were distributed throughout STN without anatomical clustering, contrasting with the restricted localization of Stop cells.
evaluation: Claims C47-C50, C70-C71 describe proactive control correlates. The behavioral evidence for proactive control is shown (C47, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), neuronal proportions are clearly stated, and the lack of anatomical clustering (Figure 8D) contrasts sharply with Stop cell localization, supporting distinct mechanisms.

result: Reactive and proactive control mechanisms are distinct in STN. No interaction was found between cell categories (χ²=1.75, p=0.42), Switch-stop cells were equally distributed between Go and NoGo categories, and NoGo activity had no predictive power for switch-signal responses.
evaluation: Claims C51-C53, C74-C75 argue for independence of reactive and proactive mechanisms. The statistical test (χ² test) is appropriate, the proportions of Switch-stop cells in Go/NoGo categories are balanced (C52), and the lack of predictive relationship is demonstrated (Figure 8E, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).

result: Control analyses showed that reward- and error-related activities did not show similar anatomical localization to Stop cells, and baseline firing rates did not differ between cell types or animals.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 present negative control findings. The lack of anatomical clustering for reward/error signals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) contrasts with Stop cell localization, and the ANOVA (F<2.13, p>0.15) appropriately tests for baseline differences. These controls strengthen the main findings.

result: The study provides the first evidence for selective encoding of reactive stopping at the cellular level in healthy primate STN, restricted to the ventromedial portion. This finding is consistent with clinical evidence implicating this region in impulse control disorders and DBS effects.
evaluation: Claims C5, C54, C67, C90-C93 present the main conclusions and clinical relevance. The novelty claims (C54, C67) are justified by the comprehensive dissociation of stopping, switching, and proactive control. The connection to clinical literature (C90-C93) is well-supported by citations and aligns with the anatomical findings.

result: Two distinct response patterns were observed among STN neurons meeting temporal criteria: Movement cells with truncated movement-related activity (most common) and cells with phasic increases to stop signals. Movement cell cancellation times were slightly earlier than Stop cells.
evaluation: Claims C56-C58 describe the two main response patterns. The patterns are clearly illustrated (Figures 3-4), the relative timing is quantified (C58), and the interpretation that Movement cells show earlier cancellation is data-driven, though it challenges simple race model predictions.

result: The ventromedial STN region containing Stop/Switch cells receives topographically organized inputs from prefrontal cortex (including IFC linked to stopping), GABAergic inputs from associative/limbic pallidum, and contained few Movement cells, making local comparison of Stop and Go processes unlikely.
evaluation: Claims C76-C80 integrate the present anatomical findings with prior connectivity literature. The citations to tract-tracing studies are appropriate (C76-C79), and the observation that this region contains few Movement cells (C80, Figure 4B) is data-driven and leads to a reasonable inference about local processing.

result: The commonly accepted model of divergent STN projections to GPi/SNr has limited anatomical support. Alternative pathways including direct and indirect STN-PPN projections may mediate stop signals, and reactive stopping likely depends on multiple pathways and cascaded processes.
evaluation: Claims C81-C87 critically evaluate prevailing models and propose alternatives. The critique of the divergence model is well-supported by anatomical citations (C83-C84), the PPN pathway proposal is grounded in anatomy and physiology (C85-C86), and the acknowledgment of multiple pathways (C87) is appropriately cautious.

result: Comparison with prior studies shows both similarities and differences. Unlike rat STN recordings where neurons responded equally to Stop and Go cues, the present study found selective responses. Human DBS studies and macaque oculomotor studies found similar selective populations.
evaluation: Claims C63-C66, C68 appropriately contextualize findings within prior literature. The contrasts with rat studies (C63-C64) and similarities with human/primate studies (C65-C66, C68) are accurately represented based on the citations. This demonstrates both novelty and consistency with relevant prior work.

result: Background claims establish that STN is hypothesized to play a central role in stopping based on neuroimaging, lesion, and DBS studies, though prior single-unit evidence was limited and potentially confounded. STN has distinct anatomical subdivisions with the ventromedial region receiving prefrontal inputs.
evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C18 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. These establish the motivation for the study, summarize prior evidence for STN involvement in stopping, and describe relevant anatomical organization. The citations appear accurate and comprehensive.

result: Interpretive claims about STN function: STN is part of attention/salience networks, NoGo cell distribution implies multiple functional sub-circuits, prior studies implicated indirect pathway in proactive control, and STN influences motor centers primarily via GPi/SNr excitation though GPe-mediated inhibition may dominate in some contexts.
evaluation: Claims C60, C72-C73, C88-C89 present interpretations and connections to broader literature. These are appropriately supported by citations and represent reasonable inferences from the data (e.g., C72 about NoGo cell distribution). The acknowledgment of alternative models (C89) shows appropriate scientific caution.

result: Ethical approval was obtained from the University of Pittsburgh IACUC (protocol 12111162) and procedures complied with Public Health Service policies.
evaluation: Claim C96 documents ethical approval. This is a straightforward statement of regulatory compliance that is standard for animal research and does not require further evaluation.
